analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to residents who buy in, with income-based premium caps.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees on June 12, 2025 with no cosponsors and no committee action since; no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state open its Medicaid program to residents who don't already qualify for Medicaid or other coverage. People who buy in would pay premiums capped at 8.5% of household income, could use the same federal premium tax credits available for marketplace plans, and would get standard cost-sharing protections. The bill also makes it easier for states that have never expanded Medicaid to get the enhanced federal matching rate, restores a Medicare-level payment floor for primary care providers treating Medicaid patients, and requires state Medicaid programs to cover comprehensive reproductive health care, including abortion.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults who earn too much for Medicaid but can't afford or don't have other coverage in states that choose to participate — they could buy into Medicaid at premiums capped at 8.5% of income, with premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions applied [S2][S3]. Primary care doctors, nurse practitioners, and community clinics gain because the bill restores a payment floor at Medicare rates for primary care services under Medicaid [S3]. States that have not expanded Medicaid gain the chance to claim the enhanced federal matching rate no matter when they expand [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Allows states, at their option, to let residents not otherwise eligible for Medicaid buy into the state Medicaid plan starting January 1, 2026 [S2][S3].

Caps total annual premiums for a family at 8.5% of household income and applies Affordable Care Act cost-sharing limits, with eligibility for federal premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions [S3].
Gives every state that expands Medicaid the enhanced federal matching rate regardless of when it expands, removing the penalty for late-expanding states [S2][S3].

Restores the requirement that Medicaid pay primary care providers no less than Medicare rates, and extends it to obstetricians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified nurse-midwives, with managed care plans required to pass those payment rates through to providers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the added cost of the enhanced Medicaid matching rate and a 90% federal match for administering the buy-in program [S3]. Private health insurers selling marketplace or employer plans would lose premium revenue in states where residents shift to the cheaper Medicaid buy-in. Employers whose plans are unaffordable could see workers move to the buy-in option.

drawbacks.text: Participation is optional for states, so coverage would only exist where a state chooses to open its Medicaid program; states with the most uninsured residents could simply decline [S2][S3].

Families could still owe premiums up to 8.5% of household income — a substantial share for middle-income households — and the buy-in coverage is limited to the Medicaid benefit package under section 1902(k)(1) [S3].

The mandate that Medicaid cover comprehensive reproductive health care including abortion would be opposed by some states on policy and funding grounds, and could make adoption of the public option less likely in those states [S3].
The bill adds ongoing federal spending through the enhanced matching rate and 90% administrative match, with $50 million appropriated for state quality-measure updates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who fall in the coverage gap between Medicaid and affordable marketplace plans, the buy-in option with capped premiums and tax credits is a direct, meaningful benefit. The cost is mainly federal matching spending, and the design deliberately leaves the choice to each state, which limits both the reach and the federal exposure. The state opt-out is the biggest weakness: in states that decline, nothing changes. The abortion-coverage mandate is a genuine political flashpoint that could reduce adoption in some states even if the buy-in itself is popular.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on June 12, 2025, and neither committee has acted on it since; no vote has been scheduled [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the State Public Option Act in the House on June 12, 2025 [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means, with no further action recorded since [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no committee action and no cosponsors, the bill's fate is effectively in the hands of committee leadership, and the status quo continues: private insurers keep the customers they would have lost to a public option, and residents without affordable coverage remain without one.

for.name: Kim Schrier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State Public Option Act on June 12, 2025; no member of either party has cosponsored it [S1][S4].

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken and no member of either party has cosponsored the bill, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record; both referral committees have taken no action [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private health insurers (marketplace and employer plans)
industries.note: A Medicaid buy-in capped at 8.5% of income, purchasable through the exchanges with premium tax credits, is a cheaper alternative that could pull customers away from marketplace and employer coverage in participating states [S3]. Insurers' interest in keeping those premium dollars runs against the interests of residents seeking lower-cost coverage.

Buy-in enrollees would be enrolled through state Medicaid managed care contracts, adding covered lives and revenue, while the bill also requires those plans to pass Medicare-level primary care payment rates through to providers [S3].

industries.industry: Primary care providers, community health centers, and clinics
industries.note: The bill restores and broadens the Medicaid payment floor at Medicare rates for family medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and certified nurse-midwives, and requires managed care entities to pay providers accordingly [S3].
More insured patients would reduce uncompensated care, but Medicaid rates are low and the primary care payment floor explicitly excludes services provided in hospital emergency departments [S3].

analysis.trajectory: A health coverage bill with no cosponsors, sitting in two committees for months with no markup or hearing scheduled, rarely reaches the floor. Unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support or leadership decides to prioritize it, the most likely path is that the bill dies in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
